WFP Burkina 
May 2026 
Contact info: Liam Wylie (liam.wylie@wfp.org) 
Country Director: ai Aline SAMU (aline.samu@wfp.org) 
 
WFP BURKINA FASO 
COUNTRY BRIEF 
May 2026 
KEY HIGHLIGHTS 
• In April, WFP assisted 415,351 people, delivering 
3,590 mt of food. This reflects a slight decrease 
compared to March, mainly due to operational 
constraints, while efforts continued to reach 
vulnerable populations. 
• Humanitarian needs remain significant, 
underscoring the importance of sustained 
assistance to protect vulnerable populations and 
consolidate recent gains. 
• WFP continues an integrated response across 
food assistance, nutrition, school meals and 
resilience, requiring USD 99.6 million for May–
October 2026 to sustain operations and avoid 
further deterioration in food security. 
IN NUMBERS

Photo Caption & Credit: WFP/Photographer Jecuthiel Yameogo 
 
SITUATION OVERVIEW 
 
• Burkina Faso faces a complex crisis driven by 
insecurity, climate shocks, and structural 
vulnerabilities. Reliance on rainfed agriculture 
heightens exposure to climate variability. Insecurity 
remains the primary driver of humanitarian needs, 
with 2 million internally displaced persons (latest 
official figure, March 2023), limiting access to land, 
markets, and essential services. 
• The preliminary results from the April 2026 national 
food security and nutrition analysis projects 1.66 
million people will face crisis-level food insecurity (IPC 
Phase 3+), including 223,000 people in emergency 
situations, during the June–August 2026 lean season, 
compared to 2.3 million in 2025. While the situation 
shows an overall improvement relative to last year, 
access constraints remain significant in several 
regions, despite localized progress observed in 2025 
such as the restoration of access to Titao and 
Barsalogho. 
• Already in 2025, funding shortfalls forced WFP to 
reduce its coverage by around 30 percent compared 
to 2024, contributing to deteriorating food 
consumption and increased negative coping 
strategies among vulnerable households. WFP 
continues to deliver an integrated response including 
emergency food and nutrition assistance, school 
feeding, resilience activities, and common services 
through UNHAS, supporting national efforts toward 
stabilization and food sovereignty.
WFP Burkina Faso Country Brief 
May 2026 
OPERATIONAL UPDATES 
General Food Assistance 
• In April, WFP distributed over 2,907 mt of food and 
nutrition assistance to 197,404 people in localities 
such as Silmague, Seguenega, and Diapaga, 
including 180 mt airlifted to localities such as 
Kantchari or Gorgadji. 
• WFP took part in two government-mandated 
convoys: one to Gayeri and another to Sebba and 
Solhan. WFP had last joined convoys to these 
locations in April 2025 and December 2024, 
respectively. 
• The main challenge remains funding constraints, 
which limit WFP’s ability to meet needs. In addition, 
two WFP airlift helicopters were unavailable due to 
operational and administrative constraints, 
significantly reducing airlift capacity and increasing 
reliance on road transport. 
Nutrition 
• WFP supported malnutrition prevention by 
assisting 855 young children and 553 women, while 
screening over 2,600 children and identifying very 
few cases of moderate malnutrition; nutrition 
awareness reached more than 4,300 people. 
• To treat moderate acute malnutrition, WFP 
provided specialized nutritious foods to over 
31,700 children and 15,600 women. 
• WFP also strengthened local production of fortified 
foods through quality audits and training for 
national producers, improving standards and 
capacity. 
School-Based Assistance 
• In April, WFP reached 236,644 students (56 percent 
girls) with daily hot meals in 755 schools, including 
7,259 students who received take-home rations 
(THR), to support attendance and retention. 
• Under the integrated programme, 171,950 
students (56 percent girls) in 629 schools received 
hot meals, with THR provided to upper primary 
students meeting attendance criteria. Under 
emergency school feeding, 64,694 students (54 
percent girls) in 126 schools were assisted, 
including 34,484 IDPs, with support limited to on-
site meals due to funding constraints. 
• Efforts focused on programme quality and capacity 
strengthening (field monitoring, partnerships, 
kitchen construction), alongside coordination with 
partners and government, including Education 
Cluster engagement and planning for the phase-
out of emergency school feeding by end-2026. 
Resilience and Livelihood Support 
• In April 2026, WFP strengthened community 
resilience through the Food Assistance for Assets 
(FFA) programme, supporting the production of 
185 compost heaps (9 m³ each), treatment of 17 
gullies, and restoration of 86 hectares of degraded 
land. Activities also included the construction of 
2,101 improved cookstoves, rehabilitation of 14 
water ponds, seedling production, and assistance 
to 2,686 beneficiaries with 266 mt of food. 
• Through the Smallholder Agricultural Market 
Support (SAMS) programme, WFP reinforced 
livelihoods by supporting farmer organization 
targeting and delivering SBCC messaging, while 
strengthening capacities through trainings of 40 
participants (13 women) on GBV/PSEA and data 
collection, alongside project staff induction and 
technical workshops. 
United Nations Humanitarian Air Service 
(UNHAS) 
• In April 2026, UNHAS supported humanitarian 
operations through 246 flights to 27 destinations, 
serving 71 user organizations, and transporting 
1,351 passengers as well as 22.9 mt of light cargo. 
Despite limited flight cancellations, UNHAS 
maintained access to isolated and hard-to-reach 
locations, including Bourzanga, Gorgadji, Arbinda, 
Djibo, and other remote areas. 
 
FUNDING OVERVIEW 
Country Strategic Plan (2019-2026) 
 
 
Donors: 
Donors to WFP’s Burkina Faso Country Strategic Plan include 
Austria, Burkina Faso, Canada, Denmark, the European 
Commission, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, 
Luxembourg, Monaco, the Netherlands, Norway, the Republic 
of Korea, the Russian Federation, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, 
the United Kingdom and the United States of America. 
Additional support was provided by the UN Central Emergency 
Response Fund (CERF) and private donors, including the Ajram 
Foundation, Buddhist Global Relief, the Gwendolyn Sexton 
Foundation, and The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day 
Saints.

related.title: Human Appeal supports Syrian farmers through new wheat supply chain project
related.summary: It was established in 1991 as a registered and regulated UK charity that runs targeted aid relief programmes in collaboration with recognised global organisations such as the United Nations. By improving access to essential agricultural inputs and reducing financial barriers, the Wheat Supply Chain project aims to increase local wheat production, enhance food security and promote long-term self-reliance, while supporting the recovery of agricultural communities across northwest Syria.
bullets: It was established in 1991 as a registered and regulated UK charity that runs targeted aid relief programmes in collaboration with recognised global organisations such as the United Nations.

By improving access to essential agricultural inputs and reducing financial barriers, the Wheat Supply Chain project aims to increase local wheat production, enhance food security and promote long-term self-reliance, while supporting the recovery of agricultural communities across northwest Syria.
Its purpose is to save and transform lives through emergency aid response and sustainable development programmes at home and abroad across over 30 countries worldwide.
The project will support over 1,000 farmers across the governorates of Aleppo, Idlib and Hama, some of Syria's most significant wheat-producing regions.
Many of the beneficiaries are among those who were displaced during years of conflict and have now returned to their communities following the end of the war.
related.excerpt: The initiative will help more than 1,000 farmers across northwest Syria rebuild livelihoods, strengthen food security and restore agricultural production as they return to their communities Manchester, UK - 14 July 2026: Human Appeal, one the UK’s leading humanitarian charities, has launched a new, localised wheat supply chain project in northwest Syria to help returning farmers restore agricultural production, protect livelihoods and support the country's long-term food security. The project will support over 1,000 farmers across the governorates of Aleppo, Idlib and Hama, some of Syria's most significant wheat-producing regions. Many of the beneficiaries are among those who were displaced during years of conflict and have now returned to their communities following the end of the war. As part of the first phase of the project, Human Appeal has covered the cost of harvesting one hectare of wheat for each participating farmer, helping to reduce immediate production costs and protect this year's harvest. In the coming months, farmers will also receive wheat seeds and fertilisers, enabling them to continue cultivating their land more sustainably and improve future yields. By improvin

related.title: Lebanon: Violence against Healthcare in Conflict 2025 [EN/AR] (pdf)
related.summary: The early 2025 United States Agency for International Development (USAID) aid freeze disrupted planned US funding flows and contributed to the reduced availability of humanitarian assistance in Lebanon, particularly for nutrition, food security, and refugee support programs. Despite a ceasefire announced on November 27, 2024, violations continued throughout 2025, resulting in civilian deaths and injuries and the widespread damaging or destruction of essential infrastructure.
bullets: The early 2025 United States Agency for International Development (USAID) aid freeze disrupted planned US funding flows and contributed to the reduced availability of humanitarian assistance in Lebanon, particularly for nutrition, food security, and refugee support programs.

Despite a ceasefire announced on November 27, 2024, violations continued throughout 2025, resulting in civilian deaths and injuries and the widespread damaging or destruction of essential infrastructure.

By September 2025, around 82,000 people remained displaced due to ongoing Israel Defense Forces (IDF) armed violence and its occupation of parts of southern Lebanon, and by October approximately 64,000 were still internally displaced, primarily from southern border areas, including Bint Jbeil, Marjayoun, and El Nabatieh.

VIOLENCE AGAINST OR OBSTRUCTION OF HEALTH CARE IN 2025 In 2025, violence against or obstruction of health care decreased dramatically in Lebanon following the ceasefire in late 2024, but overall insecurity persisted.
For the latest available figures, see Insecurity Insight’s global map on attacks on health care.

At least three health workers were killed. Methodology and sources Information on incidents of violence against health care in Lebanon is compiled from open and private sources and information projects. For the latest available figures, see Insecurity Insight’s global map on attacks on health care since 2016.

Lebanon: Violence Against Health Care Persisted in Lebanon in 2025 Despite Ceasefire Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) identified 15 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care in Lebanon in 2025, compared to 497 in 2024 and 18 in 2023.

Other resources Insecurity Insight's social media monitoring brief analyses public narratives surrounding attacks on first responders in Lebanon, and examines how rescue and health organisations were discussed across two distinct social media environments: Lebanon and Israel.

In Israel the conversation was driven by persistent narratives rather than events - volume was flat week-on-week, with little engagement with the human consequences of strikes on first responders, and a higher share of critical content.
related.excerpt: Lebanon: Violence Against Health Care Persisted in Lebanon in 2025 Despite Ceasefire Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) identified 15 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care in Lebanon in 2025, compared to 497 in 2024 and 18 in 2023. Emergency medical services were attacked on at least nine occasions and health facilities were damaged at least six times. At least three health workers were killed. Key findings: All but one of the reported incidents were attributed to the IDF, often involving drone- or aircraft-delivered strikes that damaged health facilities and ambulances or struck areas in the vicinity of hospitals. Maternal care services were disrupted when nearby IDF air strikes interrupted routine health services at a school, causing panic among children and teachers. Health needs that emerged during the conflict were further exacerbated by displacement, which restricted access to health care, placed additional strain on already overburdened health systems, limited the availability of essential medicines, and caused additional physical and psychological harm.
